lead: npm is two things at once: a public registry of JavaScript packages and the command-line tool that fetches them. Your project keeps a wish list in package.json, written as version ranges. The installer resolves those ranges against the registry, downloads code into node_modules, and records the exact versions it chose in package-lock.json. That split lets a team share one small manifest while every machine installs a repeatable set of files. You use npm in every Node project, in Express APIs, and in CI pipelines that must build the same app twice.
prereq: You need Chapter 6.1 for how require() searches node_modules, and Unit 3 for ES modules.

blocks.text: npm init -y writes a starting package.json with default answers. The file is JSON, so keys and string values need double quotes. It records what the project is and what it needs.

items: name and version identify the package. Version follows semantic versioning.
main names the entry file that require() loads when another file imports this package. An app often uses index.js or server.js.
scripts stores short commands you run with npm run.
dependencies lists packages the running app needs, such as Express.
devDependencies lists tools needed only for development or testing, such as nodemon.

blocks.text: Install a runtime package with npm install express. Add -D for a development tool: npm install -D nodemon. npm edits package.json and downloads code. A local install puts packages inside the project's node_modules folder. A global install with -g puts a command on your machine for all projects. Keep libraries local; use global only for command-line tools. Put start in scripts as node server.js, then run npm start. Other scripts run as npm run dev.

Semantic versioning writes a version as MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. MAJOR changes when old code may break. MINOR adds features without breaking old code. PATCH fixes bugs without changing behaviour. From 4.18.2 to 4.19.0 is a minor update; 4.18.2 to 4.18.3 is a patch; 4.18.2 to 5.0.0 is a major change.
A range lets npm choose a newer version that should still work. Two ranges appear in exams.

items: ^4.18.2 means at least 4.18.2 and below 5.0.0. The caret locks the major number.
~1.2.3 means at least 1.2.3 and below 1.3.0. The tilde locks the minor number.
An exact version such as 4.18.2 allows only that version.

blocks.text: Write a dependency as express set to ^4.18.2 to accept future minor and patch releases. Use ~ when you want only patch releases. Use an exact version when even a minor update is risky. npm reads these ranges, asks the registry for matching versions, and chooses one set for the project.

package-lock.json records the exact version of every installed package, plus the versions of their dependencies. package.json says ^4.18.2; the lock file may say 4.18.2 today. Commit the lock file. Then every developer and every server installs the same tree.

items: node_modules is generated. Never edit it by hand. Usually do not commit it; it is large and can be rebuilt from the manifest and lock file.
npm install reads package.json, may update versions inside the allowed ranges, and writes or updates the lock file.
npm ci deletes node_modules, installs exactly the lock file, and fails if package.json and the lock file disagree. CI pipelines use it for repeatable builds. See Chapter 6.9.
npx runs a package command without a permanent global install, for example npx nodemon server.js.

blocks.text: Run your own scripts with npm run script-name. npm start and npm test are shortcuts for the start and test scripts. Some syllabi group npm with task runners such as Grunt and Gulp; those are front-end build tools covered with the front-end unit. For a project, you need the commands above, not the whole npm CLI.

figure.caption: package.json carries the range ^4.18.2; package-lock.json and node_modules carry the exact 4.18.2.

spec.aria: A project folder holds package.json declaring express with the range ^4.18.2, a package-lock.json that pins exact versions, and node_modules holding express 4.18.2.

examples.question: A project has express set to ^4.18.2 and tool set to ~1.2.3. For Express, test 4.17.1, 4.18.2, 4.19.0 and 5.0.0. For the tool, test 1.2.9 and 1.3.0. How many versions are allowed for each range?
steps: Write the caret range ^4.18.2 as 4.18.2 ≤ version < 5.0.0.
Test 4.17.1: it is below 4.18.2, so reject it.
Test 4.18.2: it equals the lower bound, so accept it.
Test 4.19.0: it is above 4.18.2 and below 5.0.0, so accept it.
Test 5.0.0: it equals the upper bound, which is excluded, so reject it.
Write the tilde range ~1.2.3 as 1.2.3 ≤ version < 1.3.0.
Test 1.2.9: it is between the bounds, so accept it.
Test 1.3.0: it equals the upper bound, so reject it.
examples.answer: For ^4.18.2, 2 versions are allowed: 4.18.2 and 4.19.0. For ~1.2.3, 1 version is allowed: 1.2.9.

traps: Swapping ^ and ~: the caret locks the major number, the tilde locks the minor number.
Treating ^4.18.2 as allowing 5.0.0. The upper bound is excluded.
Deleting package-lock.json and expecting the same install on every machine.
Running npm install on a server when the lock file must be obeyed; that is a job for npm ci.
Editing node_modules by hand. It is generated, so the edit is lost on the next install.

quiz.a: It records the exact versions of installed packages and their dependencies, so installs can be repeated.
The lock file fixes exact versions. Every developer and server then installs the same tree instead of resolving the ranges differently.

quiz.q: Which of these versions are allowed by ^2.4.1: 2.3.9, 2.4.1, 2.5.0, 3.0.0?
quiz.a: The range is 2.4.1 ≤ version < 3.0.0. Allowed: 2.4.1 and 2.5.0. Rejected: 2.3.9 is too old, 3.0.0 is a new major version.

quiz.q: A package.json says ~1.2.3 but an installed package is 1.3.0. Is that allowed? Explain.
quiz.a: No. The tilde range is 1.2.3 ≤ version < 1.3.0. Version 1.3.0 equals the excluded upper bound, so it is outside the range.
It runs a package command without installing that package globally.

quiz.q: Why does a CI pipeline use npm ci instead of npm install?
quiz.a: npm ci deletes node_modules, installs exactly the lock file, and fails on a manifest-lock mismatch. That gives a clean, repeatable build.

quiz.q: Give one package that belongs in dependencies and one that belongs in devDependencies.
quiz.a: Express belongs in dependencies because the running app needs it. nodemon belongs in devDependencies because it is used only while developing.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real teams add npm workspaces for monorepos, private registries for company packages, and audit commands to check known vulnerabilities. Package managers such as pnpm and Yarn solve the same problem with different disk layouts and lock-file formats. Search next for npm workspaces, npm audit, and lock-file review in code review.
